explanation:
The source text of Torah #107 is exceptional among Rebbe Nachman's teachings in that it contains pure eitza reasoning from first word to last. The 5-line text proceeds as follows:

1. Opening verse (Devarim 21): 'Ki tetzei lamilchama al oyvekha' — interpreted as going out to war against the yetzer hara.
2. 'U'netano Hashem Elokekha beyadekha' — reinterpreted: the yetzer hara will hand/surrender Hashem Elokekha into your hands (i.e., through pride the yetzer causes a person to distance themselves from God).
3. 'The Torah gives advice on this' — this is an explicit eitza framing.
4. 'VeshavitaShivyo' — with the same thing it wants to overpower you (gadlut/pride), overpower it: say 'How can I rule (be a king/tzaddik) when I have gaavah (arrogance) and God does not dwell with me?'

This is a clean eitza loop: pride → use pride against pride → humility → divine presence. Not a single concept is labeled a 'bechina' of another in the 5-line text. The rich bechina content of this Torah exists only in the commentary sections (1071–1079) which are already captured in the dataset.

source_text_concepts_examined.reason: The enemy is identified as the yetzer hara via the interpretation marker 'shehu' (= 'which is'). While 'shehu' can be a bechina marker, in this text it functions as a 'hayta' (explication) that sets up the eitza reading of the verse. The identification אויב = יצר הרע is an interpretive reframing of the verse for practical advice, not a structural bechina establishing parallel nature.

Gaavah/gadlut appears in the text as the practical tool of the eitza — you use the yetzer's own gadlut against it. This is cause-and-effect: the yetzer's gadlut → your response (recognizing that gadlut prevents divine presence) → the yetzer is defeated. No bechina pairing is established.
